coach_says: White was threatening Qxg6, which is mate because your own knight on d7 takes the king's only flight square. Nb8 frees d7, but the king still gets hunted down (Qxg6+ Kd7 Qf5+ Ke8 Qe6 and mate soon). Before anything else, ask what your opponent threatens: Rf1 meets Qxg6+ with Rf7, blocking the check, and you stay in the game.

With only a queen against your pawn, your king must stay glued to the queening square and the corner. Stepping out to c6 lets Black check from d5 and drive you to b6, then Qa8 sits in front of the pawn on c8 and Black's king walks over to win it. Keep the king on b7, b8 or the a-file (Ka8, Ka7, Ka6) so that whenever you queen, Black can only trade queens and it is a draw.
also: queen blockades in front of the pawn

coach_says: Black's knight on e5 is pinned to the king by your queen on d4, so it cannot run away. Taking it at once with the bishop lets Black recapture Rxe5 with check on your king on e3, and Black's rook becomes active with tempo. With a pinned piece, pile up on it first: Nf3 develops your last minor piece and adds a third attacker, so the knight still falls later on your terms.
concept: pile up on the pinned piece

coach_says: Black's f5 pawn was asking a question, and Ng3 ignores it: Black simply plays ...f4, the knight has to go back to e2, and Black gains kingside space for ...g5-g4. Take on f5 first (exf5 Bxf5) to keep the e4 square for your pieces and stop the pawn from rolling forward. Before putting a piece on a square, check whether a pawn can kick it with tempo.

Your knight on c3 was attacked by the rook on f3 and nothing defended it. dxc4 grabs a pawn but leaves the knight hanging, and White just takes it. Nxe2+ was the clean answer: the knight escapes by capturing with check, trades itself off, and you keep your extra pawn. Always ask which of your pieces are attacked before grabbing material.
concept: left the knight on c3 hanging

coach_says: Both sides had a piece hanging: your bishop on c2 was attacked by White's queen, but White's knight on d5 was defended by nothing. Retreating with Be4 lets White save the knight with Ne3, so the chance is gone. Qxd5 wins the knight first, and after Qxc2 your queen takes on g2 and hits the rook on h1, leaving you a pawn up with White's king stuck in the centre. When pieces are hanging on both sides, look to capture before you retreat.

Qh4+ is a lone queen check that achieves nothing: g3 kicks the queen and you have to spend another move retreating it. The strong move was dxe5, because if White recaptures fxe5, then Qh4+ g3 Qe4+ forks the king and the rook on h1. Look for checks that come with a second threat, and don't bring the queen out early just to give one check.
also: Qh4+ then Qe4+ fork after dxe5

coach_says: Your bishop on d6 is already aimed at h2, and White has no knight on f3 to defend that square. Ng4 brings a second piece to h2 and threatens Qh4 with mate, and the defences cost White material (g3 Nxh2 Kxh2 Qh4+ and Qxc4 wins the bishop; h3 Bh2+ Kh1 Nxf2+ forks king and queen). The slow a5 lets White play Nd2 and Nf3 to cover. When the king has no knight on f3, look at Bd6, Ng4 and Qh4 against h2.
concept: attack h2 with Ng4 and Qh4

coach_says: The knight on c2 forked your rook and bishop, and you replied with your own grab on b7, which lets Black trade off your strong bishop with Nxe3 and win back the material. Bc5 saves the bishop with purpose: it covers f8 and e7 so Black can't castle short and the king stays in the centre, and if Black takes Nxa1, Bxb7 forks the rook on a8 and Bc6+ follows. Save the forked piece onto an active square before counter-grabbing.

Nxg5 gives a whole knight for two pawns, and after hxg5 Bxg5 the pin on f6 wins nothing back: Black just develops with ...dxc4 and ...Be7 and is a piece up. Your bishop on h4 was attacked by the g5 pawn, so simply retreat it (Bg3), or hit back first with c5 against the bishop on d6. A sacrifice needs a concrete follow-up; count what you get before giving a piece.

White's g3 pawn is pinned to the king on h2 by your queen on d6, and your knight on h5 already attacks it. Ne7 heading for f5 adds a third attacker, and White's queen and king can't hold g3 for long. Bd7 is passive and lets White play Ne5, blocking the diagonal and trading off your active pieces. When an enemy pawn is pinned, bring more pieces against it.
concept: pile up on the pinned g3 pawn

coach_says: Your queen had to move because Bg3 attacked it, but on e6 it no longer guards c7, so Bxc7 wins a pawn. It also blocks your e-pawn and your light-squared bishop and can be hit again by c4 and Nf3. Qd8 keeps c7 safe and leaves your pieces free to develop. When your queen gets chased, check which squares it was guarding before you choose where it goes.

Both your knights were attacked, and Nf6 rescues one but lets White trade on c5 and play f5 against your king. Nxe4 was stronger: after Nxe4 exf4 your pawn hits the bishop on e3 and your rook on e8 now attacks the knight on e4, so you win back the piece and come out a pawn up with an open e-file. When pieces are attacked, look for a counter-capture that opens a line for your rook.
concept: win e4 by opening the e-file

coach_says: Against a bishop and two queenside pawns, your rook needs a passed pawn of its own to win. g4! does it: if Black takes en passant, h4 gives you a passed h-pawn and the g3 pawn falls, and if not, g5 creates a passed g-pawn while Black's king is far away on b4. Kf2 is passive and gives Black time to push the b-pawn. In endgames, ask how you will make a passed pawn, and do it while the enemy king is far away.
concept: create a passed pawn with g4

coach_says: Black's pawn on e4 was attacked by your queen and nothing defended it, so Qxe4 simply wins a pawn. Bg3 lets Black play Qf5, protecting e4 and offering a queen trade, and the pawn is gone. Every move, check what your pieces attack and whether it is defended before playing a quiet move.

You are a pawn up, and Rd2+ wins another one: after the king moves, Rxh2 takes the h-pawn and your rook gets behind White's pawns. Kg6 is a reasonable king move but gives White time to tidy up. In rook endings look first for active rook moves, checks that win pawns, before quiet king moves.

The e5 pawn attacked your bishop, and recapturing with the pawn misses a tactic: Bxe5! fxe5 Qd4+ gives check and attacks the loose rook on c3, so you win the rook back. fxe5 leaves you a piece down with nothing to show. When you are behind, look for checks that hit a second, undefended piece, here the rook on c3.
concept: queen fork Qd4+ on the loose rook

coach_says: Your knight on b4 was eyeing c2, and your b7 pawn was attacked by the bishop on f3. Castling long does both jobs: the king guards b7 and your rook takes the open d-file with tempo, which also stops White castling queenside. After Bc5, White castles long himself, covers c2 and takes the d-file instead. When the d-file is open and both kings are in the centre, the first to castle onto it gains a lot.
concept: castle long to seize the d-file

coach_says: Qg5 threatens nothing real, and Black simply takes Bxh6 Qxh6 Nf5, kicking your queen while hitting d4 and h4, so you have lost time. Your bishop on h6 was going to be exchanged anyway, so take first with Bxg7 Kxg7 and then castle, keeping your queen on a good square. Don't make queen moves that can be met by trades which gain time on her.

Your rook had to leave g3, but on g5 it is attacked by Black's queen and defended only by your queen along the g-file. Ng4+ cuts that line: if fxg4, Qxg5 wins the rook, so you have to give up the exchange with Rxg4. Rg6 was safer and active, hitting e6 and the knight on h6. When a piece is defended along a line, check whether an enemy piece can block that line with tempo.
